nameStory: This moth gets its name from its caterpillar's favorite food - Virginia creeper vines that climb up trees and buildings throughout New England. The adult moth is sometimes called the Green Grapevine Sphinx because the caterpillars also munch on wild and cultivated grapes. Both host plants belong to the grape family, which explains why this sphinx has such a specific dietary preference.
description: The Virginia Creeper Sphinx is a medium-sized moth with a robust, streamlined body typical of sphinx moths (also called hawkmoths). Adults have a wingspan of about 2-3 inches and display beautiful olive-green and brown coloration that helps them blend in perfectly with tree bark during the day. Like other sphinx moths, they're strong fliers that hover at flowers to feed, often mistaken for small hummingbirds. The caterpillars are chunky green hornworms with the characteristic 'horn' on their rear end.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Forewings show distinctive olive-green base color with darker brown bands and wavy lines that feel slightly fuzzy to the touch when the moth is at rest

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Thick, torpedo-shaped body with a pointed abdomen - feels surprisingly heavy and solid if you gently handle one

idTips.label: Flight Behavior
idTips.description: Hovers at flowers like a tiny helicopter, wings beating so fast they're nearly invisible and create a soft humming sound

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized sphinx moth with body length of about 1.5 inches - roughly the size of your thumb

idTips.label: Resting Position
idTips.description: When at rest, holds wings swept back along the body like a fighter jet, pressed tight against tree bark with wings feeling papery but sturdy

habitat: Look for these moths in areas where Virginia creeper and wild grapes grow - forest edges, old stone walls, abandoned buildings, and suburban areas with mature trees. They're especially common in mixed hardwood forests and along hiking trails where Virginia creeper vines climb up oak, maple, and other deciduous trees. You'll find them from sea level up to moderate elevations throughout New England's wooded regions.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late May, looking for mates and places to lay eggs on young Virginia creeper and grape leaves.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity from June through August - best time to spot adults hovering at flowers like honeysuckle and phlox at dusk. Caterpillars are actively feeding and growing on host plants.
seasonality.fall: Late summer caterpillars pupate in the soil. A second generation of adults may emerge in September in warmer years, but activity slows significantly.
seasonality.winter: Overwintering as pupae buried in the soil beneath host plants - completely inactive and hidden underground.

funFact: Virginia Creeper Sphinx caterpillars can completely change color from green to brown in just a few hours when they're ready to pupate, helping them blend in as they search for the perfect spot to burrow underground and transform into moths.
confusionNotes: Often confused with other sphinx moths, especially the Grapevine Sphinx, but the Virginia Creeper Sphinx has more olive-green coloring while the Grapevine Sphinx tends to be more brownish-gray. Memory trick: Virginia creeper vines turn bright green in summer, just like this moth's dominant wing color.
contextualKnowledge: Virginia creeper is often confused with poison ivy by hikers, but it's actually harmless and provides important food for this beautiful moth. The plant has five leaflets compared to poison ivy's three - 'leaves of five, let it thrive' is a helpful saying for identifying the moth's host plant safely.
compareHints: Since this is the only Darapsa species commonly found in New England, compare it to other sphinx moths in the region. It's smaller and more green-tinted than the big Tobacco Hornworm Moths, and lacks the pink and yellow coloring of the popular Hummingbird Clearwing Moths. The Virginia Creeper Sphinx has a more muted, bark-like appearance that makes it a master of camouflage.
